name: Buckling
seoDesc: Buckling: work out area moment of inertia (I) from the area of cross-section and the length of column. A free physics calculator with the formula, units…
summary: Give the Buckling calculator the area of cross-section, the length of column, the critical slenderness ratio and the critical load (F) and it returns area moment of inertia (I). It is built for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Buckling calculator work?
sections.html:
The Buckling calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports area moment of inertia (I) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the boundary condition and the material); then you type in the area of cross-section (A), the length of column (L), the critical slenderness ratio (Scriₜ) and the critical load (F) (Euler's formula).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.html:

  • A measured quantity, entered by default in square meters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 24 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in meters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 34 supported units.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 8 options, such as Al6061-O, Al2024-T3 and Al1100-H12. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.

2 fields on this form are a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Buckling calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Area moment of inertia (I)=critical load (F) × (effective length factor (K) ^ 2) × (length of column (L) ^ 2) ÷ ((PI ^ 2) × young modulus (E))
Effective length factor (K)=effective length (Lₑ) ÷ length of column (L)
Area moment of inertia (I)=area of cross-section (A) × (radius of gyration (R) ^ 2)
Slenderness ratio (S)=effective length (Lₑ) ÷ radius of gyration (R)
Yield stress (σγ)=2 × (PI ^ 2) × young modulus (E) ÷ (critical slenderness ratio (Scriₜ) ^ 2)
Yield stress (σγ)=2 × PI × radius of gyration (R) × (PI × area of cross-section (A) × radius of gyration (R) × young modulus (E) + the square root of (area of cross-section (A) × young modulus (E) × ((PI ^ 2) × area of cross-section (A) × (radius of gyration (R) ^ 2) × young modulus (E) − critical load (F) × (effective length (Lₑ) ^ 2)))) ÷ (area of cross-section (A) × (effective length (Lₑ) ^ 2))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Second moment of area, opening in quartic meters
  • Area, opening in square meters
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Pressure, opening in gigapascals
  • Pressure, opening in megapascals
  • Force, opening in newtons

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Buckling calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the area of cross-section, the length of column and the critical slenderness ratio — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Buckling calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns area moment of inertia (I), derived from the area of cross-section, the length of column and the critical slenderness ratio. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Buckling calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the area of cross-section, the length of column, the critical slenderness ratio and the critical load (F), which is 7 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter area moment of inertia (I) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Area moment of inertia (I) opens in quartic meters and the chip beside it offers 5 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Effective length factor (K) = 0. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Buckling calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
